summary:
Masovian Voivodeship stands under Poland's national framework. Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor to Poland. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals; her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

Anti-LGBT local governance, once widespread, has been dismantled through the courts and through municipal withdrawal. By January 2020 a third of Poland's territory had passed anti-LGBT resolutions. On 6 February 2024 the Voivodeship Administrative Court in Warsaw, which sits in Masovian Voivodeship, repealed the last document 'against LGBT ideology' in Poland, and by 24 April 2025 every anti-LGBTQ resolution and Family Charter endorsement had been withdrawn or court-invalidated. No such resolution is currently in force in Masovian Voivodeship.

The capital's own position has run in the opposite direction since March 2019, when Warsaw Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski signed the city's pledge of equality, non-discrimination and hate-crime response. The declaration stands and no repeal is recorded, giving a visitor in Warsaw a documented municipal commitment that contrasts with the national picture.

The wider legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Donald Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.
tangentialFactors:
The repeal of anti-LGBT resolutions was driven by administrative litigation rather than by legislative repeal, which means reversals at municipal level remain legally possible and would again be contested in the Voivodeship Administrative Court in Warsaw. The concentration of the final rulings in Masovian Voivodeship makes the province the principal forum for this litigation nationally.

Warsaw's 2019 equality declaration and the national trend toward withdrawal of anti-LGBT documents point in the same direction, while the slow pace of the Tusk government's reform programme and the postponed Penal Code amendments point the other way. Human Rights Watch's assessment that reform through 2024 was insufficient sets the realistic expectation: procedural movement without settled statutory protection.

International litigation has been more effective than domestic legislation. Two European Court of Human Rights judgments in 2024, on hormone therapy in custody and on the absence of partnership recognition, established positions that Polish authorities had not adopted on their own initiative.

Global Affairs Canada's advisory places sexual orientation alongside physical appearance and foreigner status as reported motives for harassment, which suggests the risk framing for visitors blends identity with general visibility as a foreign national.
localsOnly:
Residents of Masovian Voivodeship live with no anti-LGBT resolution in force: every such document and Family Charter endorsement in Poland had been withdrawn or court-invalidated by 24 April 2025, the last one falling to the Voivodeship Administrative Court in Warsaw on 6 February 2024.

Warsaw residents are covered by the equality, non-discrimination and hate-crime response pledge signed by Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski in March 2019, which remains in force with no recorded repeal, and can expect municipal procedures for reporting hate incidents that the pledge commits the city to answer.

Same-sex couples resident in Poland gained the ability to have marriage certificates obtained abroad recognised after Justice Minister Bodnar revoked his predecessor Ziobro's blocking directive in June 2024, though a domestic partnership framework remained absent when the European Court of Human Rights ruled in September 2024 that the resulting legal vacuum was unlawful.

Trans residents in Polish custody retain a litigable right to hormone replacement therapy under the European Court of Human Rights judgment of 11 July 2024, which awarded EUR 8,000, but placement remains individual and Poland operates no specialised trans prison section.

Penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence depend on Penal Code amendments whose status remained unsettled after approval was postponed and a second bill was introduced in late October 2024; the Prosecutor General's special response team and its law-enforcement guidelines are the operative protection machinery in the meantime.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the March and October 2024 Penal Code amendments at the time of travel is unresolved in the sources and should be verified against the current text of the Code rather than assumed from the 2024 reporting.

No source in this inventory reports statistics on reported and prosecuted hate crimes in Masovian Voivodeship, on enforcement of the Prosecutor General's guidelines, or on outcomes for trans complainants in the province; their absence is a gap in the record, not an indication that incidence is low.

Whether the enforcement mechanism behind Warsaw's 2019 declaration has been resourced or reorganised under the current city administration is not sourced here.

The sources do not establish whether every municipality in Masovian Voivodeship that had passed an anti-LGBT resolution withdrew it voluntarily or was compelled by court order, nor whether any replacement language on 'family protection' has been adopted locally after the April 2025 cutoff.

No Masovian-specific account of police treatment of trans detainees or of access to gender-affirming care in provincial health facilities is available in this inventory; the documented detention cases are national in origin.
